title: Long-haired Owl Visitor Trying to Take a Nap
summary: A Long-eared Owl tried to sleep through an October day while jays kept mobbing it. Christian shooed them off twice, took a few photos and clips, and left the owl to its nap.

fieldNotes:
I was working and heard a racket out side from a lot of bluejays and when I went outside there was an long-haired howl in my tree. I shooed away the other birds and the owl seemed to let me do it without leaving. I took a few photos and videos and went inside. Came out later to another racket in the yard, different tree same owl and also shooed away those birds and now it's still out there trying to sleep. 

This bird is an adult Long-eared Owl (Asio otus).Species IdentificationFacial Disc & Feather Tufts: It shows the signature tall, erect "ear tufts" set close together near the center of the crown, a distinct rufous/orange-buff facial disc, and white vertical facial markings outlining a dark central crease between striking yellow-orange eyes.   Slender Profile: The narrow body posture—especially when compressed against a limb in a cryptic roosting pose—is a textbook Long-eared Owl defensive behavior designed to mimic a broken branch.   Age: AdultPlumage Condition: This individual has fully developed, crisp contour feathers with defined herringbone barring and vertical streaks down the breast and flanks.   Juvenile Contrast: Downy nestlings and recently fledged branchers retain soft, fluffy, gray down plumage and much smaller, poorly defined ear tufts. By late summer and fall, birds undergo a post-juvenile molt into adult-like contour feathers; this bird has completely cleared the downy juvenile stage. Distinguishing a second-year bird from an older adult in the field typically requires examining primary feather molt patterns and ultraviolet porphyria pigment under the wing in hand.Sex: Likely Male (with caveats)Plumage Tone: Long-eared Owls show subtle plumage dimorphism. Males average distinctly paler, grayer on the back and mantle, with cleaner white backgrounds across the underparts, whereas females tend to be darker, heavier barred, and noticeably more ochre or buff-washed overall. This owl displays a relatively pale, silvery-gray cast and bright facial highlights, which points toward a male.   Size & Certainty: In owls, females are noticeably larger and heavier than males (reverse sexual size dimorphism). Without another bird perched beside it for direct scale or a bird in hand to measure wing chord and weight, visually determining sex in the field is rarely 100% conclusive.

post.title: An Owl Trying to Take a Nap
post.body:
Just before noon I heard a racket outside, a lot of jays all yelling at once. When I went out to see what it was about, there was an owl sitting in the tree, tall and narrow, with two long ear tufts standing straight up.

I shooed the jays away. The owl let me do it and didn't leave. It just looked down at me with those yellow-orange eyes. I took a few photos and a couple of videos, then went back inside and left it alone.

## Round two

In the afternoon, around twenty to four, there was another racket. Different tree, same owl, and more jays, a mix of them this time, giving it a hard time. I shooed those off too and filmed a few more short clips: the owl holding its ground, then alert and looking around once things quieted down. When I last checked, it was still out there, trying to get some sleep.

## The ID

I had an AI tool help me with the ID: it's an adult Long-eared Owl (Asio otus). The giveaways are the tall ear tufts set close together near the middle of the crown, the rusty orange facial disc, and the white lines framing a dark crease between the eyes. The breast and flanks have crisp vertical streaks and fine barring, fully grown-in adult feathers with no downy juvenile fluff left.

The way it sat is classic for the species too. When a Long-eared Owl feels watched, it pulls its feathers in tight and stretches tall and thin against a limb, so it looks more like a broken branch than a bird. Long-eared Owls roost by day and hunt at night, so all that daytime shouting is the last thing it wanted.

> When a Long-eared Owl feels watched, it pulls its feathers in tight and stretches tall and thin against a limb, so it looks more like a broken branch than a bird.

## Let it sleep

What I learned: when songbirds gang up and scold like that, it's worth stepping outside to look. It's called mobbing, and it's often how you find an owl that would otherwise be invisible. Then the best thing to do is get a few photos and let it sleep.

episode.title: The owl who wanted a nap
episode.script:
Narrated by Robot Marley.

It was a bright October day, just before noon, the leaves just starting to turn yellow, when the jays started shouting.

Not one or two of them. A whole crowd, all yelling at once. Christian went outside to see what the fuss was about.

There, up in a tree, sat an owl.

***

It was tall and narrow, with two long ear tufts standing straight up like a pair of feathered antennas. Its face was a warm rusty orange, and it looked down at him with round yellow-orange eyes.

A Long-eared Owl. An adult, in crisp grown-up feathers, streaked and barred down the front like tree bark.

The jays were mobbing it. Small birds do that when they find an owl by day. They gather and scold until it moves along. And an owl that hunts all night would very much like to be left alone in the daytime.

So Christian shooed the jays away.

Here's the small detail I love. The owl let him. It didn't fly off. It just sat there and watched him do it, as if it understood who was on its side.

He took a few photos, and then he did the harder thing. He went back inside and let it be.

***

In the afternoon, around twenty to four, there was another racket.

Different tree. Same owl. More jays, a whole mix of them, giving it a hard time.

Out went Christian again, and off went the jays. He filmed a few short clips this time. The owl holding its ground. The owl pulled tall and thin against a limb, the way Long-eared Owls do when they want to look like a broken branch instead of a bird. And then the owl, alert, looking around once the quiet came back.

That's a good eye, by the way. Plenty of people would hear the noise and never look up. Christian heard the noise and knew to go find out what it meant.

***

The last time he checked, the owl was still out there.

Trying, very patiently, to take a nap.

Some visitors don't need anything from you but a little quiet. This one got it.
